items.stem: Attitude indicator shows 15° left bank and 10° nose-up. Heading indicator reads 180. The airplane is
choices: A) climbing in a left turn toward south
B) descending in a left turn toward south
C) climbing in a right turn toward north
D) in level flight heading east
items.explanation: Left bank + nose up + 180 = climbing left turn, nose south.

items.stem: More brown than blue visible on a standard AI (ground on the bottom of the case) generally indicates
items.explanation: Nose-down shows more ground (brown) in the window.

items.stem: Fastest reliable elimination method on IC items is to first discard choices that
choices: A) have the wrong manufacturer paint scheme
B) get the bank side wrong
E) face left on the page
items.explanation: Bank side is binary and visible immediately. Use it to kill half the silhouettes.

items.stem: Heading 315 is
items.explanation: 270 west + 45° = 315 northwest.

items.stem: In a 2×2×2 cube made of 8 identical blocks, how many blocks share a FACE with one corner block?
items.explanation: A corner cube has 3 faces inward: one along each axis.

items.stem: In a solid 3×3×3 cube of 27 blocks, how many blocks share a face with the very center block?
items.explanation: The core cube has six faces, each touching one neighbor.

items.stem: A stack has a 3×3 base (9 blocks) fully filled and a 2×2 square centered on top. How many blocks are in the stack?
items.explanation: 9 + 4 = 13. No hidden third layer.

items.stem: On a 3×3×1 flat layer of 9 blocks, how many face-neighbors does the center block have?
items.explanation: Four orthogonal faces (N/E/S/W). Corners share only an edge, not a face.

items.stem: When a drawing hides interior cubes, you should assume
choices: A) hidden cubes do not exist
B) cubes float if not drawn
C) the stack is solid unless a gap is clearly shown
D) only the top layer counts
items.explanation: Standard convention: no floating unsupported blocks; fill what the geometry requires.

items.stem: Two cubes that touch only along an edge (not a full face) count as how many face-adjacencies?
items.explanation: Touching means shared FACE. Edge or corner does not count.

items.stem: Table excerpt: X headers −2, −1, 0, 1, 2. Y=3 row values: 11, 18, 24, 31, 40. What is the value at X=1, Y=3?
items.explanation: X=1 is the fourth header. Corresponding value 31.

items.stem: Same table: X headers −2, −1, 0, 1, 2. Y=3 row: 11, 18, 24, 31, 40. Value at X=−2, Y=3?
items.explanation: First column.

items.stem: The most common TR error is
choices: B) swapping X and Y or dropping one column
D) leaving items blank because of the guessing penalty
items.explanation: Axis swap and off-by-one dominate misses.

items.stem: Target pace for Table Reading is about
items.explanation: 40 items / 7 minutes ≈ 10.5 seconds.

items.stem: Y=−1 row values under X = −1, 0, 1 are 7, 9, 14. What is (X,Y) = (0, −1)?
items.explanation: Middle of those three values.

items.stem: Best TR procedure is
choices: A) scan randomly until the number 'looks right'
B) lock one axis, then the other, same order every item
C) memorize the whole table first
E) add X and Y instead of looking up
items.explanation: Consistent axis order prevents most misses.

items.stem: You discover a close friend's qualification record was signed off without the required event. MOST effective action?
choices: B) Quietly fix the form yourself without telling anyone.
C) Tell the friend to get the event done and notify the supervisor so the record is corrected.
D) Post about it in the group chat.
E) Wait until someone else notices.
items.explanation: Integrity + safety + lowest proper level: fix the real qualification and inform the person who owns the program.

items.stem: Same scenario (unsigned required event). LEAST effective action?
choices: A) Help the friend schedule the missing event today.
B) Inform the supervisor after telling the friend.
C) Ignore it because the friend is competent in practice.
D) Review whether others have the same paperwork hole.
items.explanation: Hiding a false qual is the integrity and safety failure.

items.stem: A subordinate is late twice in a week and looks exhausted. MOST effective first move?
choices: B) Talk privately, find out what is going on, reset the standard.
C) Ignore it until it becomes a pattern of months.
E) Joke about it so the team hears the hint.
items.explanation: Private fact-finding plus a clear standard. No public humiliation, no instant nuclear option.

items.stem: Your NCOIC and your officer boss give conflicting lawful-looking directions on a non-emergency task. MOST effective?
choices: C) Tell both you have a conflict and ask them to align, starting with the person who gave the later order.
D) Email the wing commander first.
items.explanation: Surface the conflict to the people who own it. Do not skip to the wing for a routine clash.

items.stem: You see an unsafe act on the line that could injure someone in the next minute. MOST effective?
choices: A) Write a memo after shift.
B) Stop the act immediately, then notify the appropriate supervisor.
C) Film it first for evidence.
D) Assume they have a waiver.
E) Ask a peer if they also think it looks bad, then decide.
items.explanation: Imminent harm: stop it, then report. Process comes second.

items.stem: You finished your work early. A peer in another shop is drowning in a time-critical task you are qualified to help with. MOST effective?
choices: A) Leave so you are not given more work.
B) Offer help after checking with your supervisor if the tasking lines require it.
C) Take over the peer's job unasked and send them home.
D) Critique their inefficiency in the group chat.
E) Only help if they will owe you a favor.
items.explanation: Service and excellence, without going freelance around your own chain.
